newsitem.title: USA: Fishery talks fail to settle US, Canada salmon row.
newsitem.headline: Fishery talks fail to settle US, Canada salmon row.

text.p: The U.S. State Department said Monday that talks between the U.S. and Canadian fishery interests failed to resolve differences over Pacific salmon fishing.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the groups representing Pacific salmon fishery interests on both sides of the border made progress in "framing and narrowing the relevant issues" but were unable to come up with agreed recommendations for their governments.

Burns said that U.S. stakeholders proposed reducing harvests of Nass-Skeena River sockeye at Noyes Island and off Fraser River sockeye. They also proposed development of a sophisticated approach to the management of wild coho salmon originiating from British Columbia and Washington, he said.

"This regime would contribute greatly to ensuring sustainable fisheries and protecting wild stocks in both countries," Burns said in a statement. "It is regrettable that despite their best efforts, the stakeholders were unable to develop agreed recommendations."
He said representatives from the two governments will meet on May 20 to consider reports from the stakeholders groups and to work on fishing regimes for 1997.

The United States and Canada have been arguing for years over how to divide up dwindling salmon stocks. The two sides have been unable to agree on implementation of the principles of a 1985 Pacific Salmon Treaty. Tensions have risen in recent years with both sides accusing the other of overfishing.
The stakeholder talks began in February with the hope that the fishery groups could settle some of the issues that defied resolution over the years.
